\Section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A roadblock to the adoption of program verification is the \emph{cost of manual specification}.
Developers care about high-level properties, e.g., that a call chain aborts only under stated preconditions, an entrypoint satisfies its postconditions, stored data respects an invariant.
But to prove any of them, the supporting functions need their own contracts, which are often boilerplate, as they restate what the code does.
\emph{Specification inference} derives such contracts from the program automatically, so that developers instead spend effort on the properties worth stating manually.
The classical engine for mechanical inference is Dijkstra's weakest-precondition analysis (\WP)~\cite{dijkstra1975wp}: propagated backward through a function, it yields the exact abort condition and the exact postcondition. However, it depends on loop invariants to provide an induction hypothesis~\cite{BL05}, and despite a long history of research~\cite{CousotHalbwachs78}, there is no complete technique for synthesizing them.

This paper describes a novel combination of agentic specification inference and mechanical weakest-precondition analysis.
An LLM agent conducts the inference, supplies loop invariants, and calls \WP and the verifier as tools.
The approach is implemented for the Move smart contract language, which is similar to safe Rust, especially in its reference semantics.
Move has strong verification support through the Move Prover (\MVP)~\cite{DillGPQXZ22,GrieskampEtAl26HO}.
Due to Move's reference semantics, \MVP can eliminate references~\cite{DillGPQXZ22}.
We run classical \WP on the reference-eliminated Move bytecode and restate its result in the predicate calculus of the specification language, over the original references.
\WP is fully modular because of \emph{behavioral predicates}~\cite{GrieskampEtAl26HO}, which let a specification refer to the contract of another function as a black box.

We evaluate our combination on a corpus of 26 inference targets.
Twenty-four of these targets are extracted from public Move code of the Aptos framework.
These have no prior specifications: a model may have seen this code during training, but it cannot recall a specification that did not exist.
We compare three tactics:
\textit{agent-only}, in which the agent works without the \WP tool;
\textit{hybrid-guided}, in which it follows a prescribed workflow that starts with \WP;
and \textit{hybrid-flexible}, in which it decides itself whether and when to call \WP.
We run each tactic under two models of one family, the frontier model Sol~5.6 and the mid-tier model Terra~5.6.
Completeness is checked with withheld mutants.

Agent-only already does well: it completes 99\% of its runs under the frontier model and 93\% under the mid-tier model.
The two hybrid tactics reach about the same completeness at 11--21\% lower cost.
The saving comes from the targets without loops, where \WP derives the complete contract, and thus the hybrids cost 36--60\% of agent-only.
On the loop targets, the agent still has to find the invariants, and the quantified \WP output adds to the context it re-reads on every turn, so the hybrids cost 9--22\% more on average.
The mid-tier model costs 53--59\% as much as the frontier model.
It falls behind mainly on one target, whose contract needs a permutation argument proved with lemmas.
Under hybrid-guided, the mid-tier model completes 97 of 104 runs; the frontier model under agent-only completes 103 but costs more than twice as much.

\Paragraph{Contributions}
Our paper makes the following contributions:
\begin{Itemize}
\item A \WP analysis over reference-eliminated Move bytecode, whose derived conditions are carried back to the references and global resources of the source, with state labels naming the intermediate memories of a function (\S~\ref{sec:wp}).
\item \WP output designed to be read by an agent rather than passed to a solver: loop-invariant evidence from bounded unrolling, and markers for conditions that are expensive for the solver or incomplete because a callee lacks a contract (\S~\ref{sec:diagnostics}).
\item The combination of the \WP analysis with a coding agent, delivered as a plugin of skills, hooks, and tools, in which the agent supplies what \WP cannot (\S\S~\ref{sec:example} and~\ref{sec:skills}).
\item An evaluation on 26 targets, mostly from real-world code, under three tactics and two models, in which an inferred contract counts as complete only if it kills every withheld mutant (\S~\ref{sec:evaluation}).
\end{Itemize}

The Move Prover was developed for the Diem project\Anon{ and has been maintained by Aptos Labs since 2022; it}{ and} has verified Diem's payment system and critical components of the Aptos blockchain~\cite{ParkZGXGCLC24,AptosFrameworkBook}.
